comparison: Perfect alignment on synthetic benchmarking results (C36, C54-C60). Both evaluations support the performance claims with OpenEval noting systematic testing across 20 repetitions and multiple conditions, while peer reviewers confirm extensive comparisons showing GromovMatcher performs well. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect alignment on EPIC validation results (C74-C82). OpenEval notes the comparison methodology is questionable since M2S and metabCombiner receive validation data for tuning while GM does not, making GM's performance more impressive. Peer reviewers acknowledge the validation without raising this fairness concern.

Perfect alignment on CS-PC results (C83-C89). Both evaluations support the finding that automated methods identify correct matches beyond expert manual matching. OpenEval notes small numbers limit statistical confidence, while peer reviewers accept this as demonstrating the value of automated methods.

Strong alignment on methodological advantages (C63-C66). Both evaluations support claims about GM's use of correlation structures versus intensity magnitudes. OpenEval provides detailed explanation with reference to Figure 3-supplement 2, while peer reviewers identify this as a main strength distinguishing GM from other methods.

Strong alignment on validation methodology (C49, C51-C53). Both evaluations support the synthetic validation approach. OpenEval notes M2S receives optimization advantages that may not reflect real-world performance, while peer reviewers accept the dataset split procedure as valid without raising this concern. OpenEval also addresses C133 not covered by peer review.

Strong alignment on limitations of existing methods (C25-C26). Both evaluations support these claims. Peer reviewers explicitly state the two main shortcomings identified by authors, while OpenEval notes these are demonstrated through comparative benchmarking. OpenEval also addresses C4 which peer review includes in broader background context (R10).

Strong alignment on core methodology and innovation (C5-C6, C38, C40-C42, C105). Both evaluations support the GromovMatcher approach. Peer reviewers emphasize innovation and effectiveness across all three reviewers, while OpenEval validates the mathematical framework and fundamental assumptions. OpenEval covers additional technical claims (C38, C107, C110) not explicitly addressed by peer review.

Strong alignment on two-dataset limitation (C96-C99). Both evaluations support the acknowledgment of this limitation. OpenEval notes the sequential alignment approach demonstrates addressability, while peer reviewers express confidence in future implementation. OpenEval also addresses C100-C101, C103 regarding population differences and solutions not explicitly covered by peer review.

Partial alignment on biomarker discovery application. Both support the alcohol biomarker findings (C92-C95). Peer reviewers confirm identification of additional features connected to alcohol consumption. OpenEval provides more detail about statistical corrections and notes lack of biological validation for new features. OpenEval also addresses C91 and C10/C37 which peer review discusses separately (R5 for application utility).

Strong alignment on background and context claims (C1-C2, C11-C16). Both evaluations support these as well-established facts about LC-MS metabolomics capabilities and applications. Peer review R10 also covers C3-C4, C17, C20-C21 regarding limitations, which OpenEval addresses separately in R2 and R3.

Partial alignment on LC-MS limitations (C3, C17, C20-C21). Both evaluations support these as established challenges. Peer review R10 groups these with broader background context (C1-C2, C4, C11-C16), while OpenEval treats limitations as a separate evaluation focused on motivating automated alignment methods.

Partial alignment on main contributions (C7-C8). Both evaluations support the summary claims. Peer reviewers emphasize innovation and validation as convincing, while OpenEval provides detailed substantiation through synthetic benchmarking, EPIC validation, and practical utility. OpenEval also addresses C10, C37, C104 which peer review discusses in context of biomarker application (R5).

Partial alignment on validation challenges (C9). Both evaluations support the field-wide challenge of lacking manually curated datasets. Peer review R7 focuses on accepting the synthetic validation solution, while OpenEval notes the limitation of relying on a single real dataset (EXPOsOMICS) for generating synthetic pairs.

OpenEval supports claims about optimal transport prior work and applications (C28-C33, C113) with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these technical background claims about Gromov-Wasserstein distance and its applications in genomics.

OpenEval supports practical algorithmic features (C111-C112, C115, C117, C119-C120) regarding handling of partial overlap, RT drift, and method variants. No corresponding peer review evaluation found explicitly addressing these implementation details, though peer reviewers generally affirm the algorithm is clearly described.

OpenEval supports EPIC data description and prior work (C67-C73) with appropriate citations. Notes validation set is relatively small (90 features for CS-HCC positive mode). No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing the EPIC dataset characteristics, though peer reviewers discuss EPIC validation results in R3.

OpenEval supports preprocessing and statistical analysis procedures (C134-C137, C143-C149) as sound methodology for biomarker discovery application. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these technical methodological details.

OpenEval supports accurate description of prior work from Loftfield et al. (C138-C142) providing context for pooled analysis comparison. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing this specific prior work citation.
